forces seen with running, altered GI blood flow, and GI motility, along 
with neuroendocrine changes from training can cause changes in 
GI function. In addition, pretraining and precompetition diet changes, 
stress, climate, dehydration, NSAID use, and bowel movements before 
exercise are some of the possible causes.
Assessment tools used to rule out food-related issues include (1) a 
thorough dietary analysis including an analysis of foods, fluids, alcohol 
use, and supplements consumed before, during and after training; 
(2) food sensitivity or allergy testing to determine whether food intoler-
ances to gluten, lactose, or other foods or herbals exist; (3) a bowel 
function and chronic GI disease history; (4) a history of overall fluid intake 
and possible dehydration because of changes in training climate; and 
(5) a history of infections and antibiotic use.
A game plan including an elimination diet if necessary, specific com-
petition day diet and fueling guidelines, and a GI healing supplementa-
tion regimen including probiotics, digestive enzymes, electrolytes, and 
vitamins and minerals is useful and reassuring for the athlete with 
GI issues (see Chapter 28).
